For information or documents related to occupational safety and health topics, you can contact NIOSH at 1-800-CDC-INFO (1-800-232-4636). The question of whether occupational exposure to engineered nanoparticles poses an unintended risk of adverse health effects is not a theoretical debate that can be postponed for years. Nanotechnology is already a reality, with significant potential for growth in the 21st century. Workers are currently involved in processes where they may be exposed to materials that have never existed in nature before. The pathways through which these engineered nanoparticles may enter the body, their distribution once inside, and their effects on various bodily systems remain largely unknown. Additionally, it is unclear whether the health effects differ for nanoparticles with varying chemical or structural properties. Stakeholders from diverse fields agree that research addressing these questions is critical for the responsible development of nanotechnology. As research progresses, NIOSH has recommended interim precautionary measures to reduce work-related exposures and assess potential risks. Within the hierarchy of prevention, it is essential to evaluate the value of medical screening for workers who may be exposed to potential health hazards but remain asymptomatic—that is, they show no identifiable symptoms of occupational disease. In the emerging field of nanotechnology, where data for confidently assessing risks is still limited, it is challenging to recommend specific screening tests. NIOSH has sought input from a wide range of experts and, along with its own review of the scientific literature, has developed interim guidance for medical screening and hazard surveillance. The body of evidence on the health effects of engineered nanoparticles is rapidly expanding, and NIOSH will continue to monitor and assess this evidence, updating its recommendations as more definitive information becomes available. Concerns have been raised about whether workers exposed to engineered nanoparticles face an increased risk of adverse health effects. The current evidence base regarding the potential health risks of occupational exposure to engineered nanoparticles is limited. While laboratory studies on animals suggest that exposure to certain engineered nanoparticles can cause adverse health effects, no health studies have been published on workers exposed to the few nanoparticles tested in animals. The purpose of this document from NIOSH is to provide interim guidance on whether specific medical screening, including tests for asymptomatic workers, is appropriate for those exposed to engineered nanoparticles. Medical screening is only one component of a comprehensive safety and health management program. An ideal program follows a hierarchy of controls and incorporates various occupational health surveillance measures. Since specific medical screening for asymptomatic workers exposed to engineered nanoparticles has not been extensively discussed in the scientific literature, this document offers recommendations based on current knowledge until more rigorous research can be conducted. At present, there is insufficient scientific and medical evidence to recommend specific medical screening for workers potentially exposed to engineered nanoparticles. However, this lack of evidence does not preclude employers from implementing specific medical screening measures as a precautionary step beyond existing industrial hygiene practices. If nanoparticles are composed of a chemical or bulk material for which medical screening recommendations already exist, those same recommendations would apply to workers exposed to the engineered nanoparticles. As research into the hazards of engineered nanoparticles continues, ongoing reassessment of available data is essential to determine whether specific medical screening is warranted for workers. In the interim, NIOSH provides the following recommendations for workplaces where workers may be exposed to engineered nanoparticles: 1. Implement prudent measures to control exposures to engineered nanoparticles. 2. Conduct hazard surveillance to inform the implementation of controls. 3. Continue using established medical surveillance approaches. NIOSH will continue to collect and evaluate new research findings and update its recommendations on medical screening programs for workers exposed to nanoparticles. Nanotechnology involves innovative methods for controlling and manipulating matter at the near-atomic scale to produce engineered materials, structures, and devices. At these scales, materials often exhibit unique properties that affect their physical, chemical, and biological behavior. These properties may differ significantly from those observed at the chemical or bulk level. Engineered nanoparticles may be intentionally manufactured or incidentally produced during processes such as combustion, welding, or diesel engine operation. It is currently unclear whether distinctions in particle terminology are justified from a safety and health perspective if the particles share the same physicochemical characteristics. The potential occupational health risks associated with the manufacture and use of nanomaterials are not yet fully understood. Exposure to these materials during manufacturing and use may occur through inhalation, dermal contact, or ingestion, with inhalation being the primary route of concern. There is very limited information available about dominant exposure routes, the potential for exposure, and material toxicity. Society and companies face the challenge of balancing the desire to expand a promising technology with the potential hazards it may pose. The real risks of nanotechnology are not yet known, and the perceived risks remain undetermined. In this regard, nanotechnology is no different from other emerging technologies. One of the first areas where exposure to engineered nanoparticles will occur is in the workplace. In the face of uncertainty about the hazards of nanoparticles, implementing appropriate occupational health surveillance measures may reassure the public that efforts are being made to identify and control potential hazards in a timely manner. Concerned individuals from government, industry, labor, academia, and the medical community have raised questions about whether workers exposed to engineered nanoparticles should undergo some form of medical surveillance. The purpose of this document is to provide interim guidance on specific medical screening for these workers, including tests for asymptomatic individuals, until additional research either supports or negates the need for such screening. The type and degree of screening recommended here are in addition to any medical surveillance already in place as part of existing occupational health efforts. Medical examinations and tests are commonly used in workplaces to determine whether an employee can perform essential job functions without posing a direct and imminent threat to their own safety or the safety of others. Workplace medical examinations must comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA), which prohibits making a job offer contingent upon the applicant's submission to a medical examination. However, pre-placement medical examinations can provide useful baseline information in various ways. For example, even if there is no immediate concern about exposure to engineered nanoparticles in a particular workplace, baseline data may benefit employers and workers if questions arise later about potential health problems associated with specific nanoparticles. Medical surveillance of workers is also required by law when there is exposure to a specific workplace hazard. Although OSHA does not have a standard specifically addressing occupational exposure to engineered nanoparticles, it has several standards requiring medical surveillance of workers. Workplaces with engineered nanoparticles composed of chemicals covered by current OSHA standards are subject to those standards, including medical surveillance requirements. NIOSH also recommends medical surveillance, including screening, for workers exposed to certain occupational hazards. While none of the hazards listed in NIOSH recommendations are specifically identified as engineered nanoparticles, medical surveillance would apply to workers exposed to nanoparticles composed of chemicals for which NIOSH has a recommendation. This surveillance may provide useful information if questions arise in the future about the health effects of exposure to nanoparticles. Hazard surveillance involves identifying potentially hazardous practices or exposures in the workplace and assessing their link to workers. The current evidence base on the possible health risks of occupational exposures to engineered nanoparticles is insufficient to support specific medical screening to identify preclinical changes associated with such exposures. No substantial link has been established between occupational exposure to engineered nanoparticles and adverse health effects. Additionally, toxicological research to date is insufficient to recommend such monitoring, determine appropriate triggers for it, or define its components. As research on the potential health effects of exposure to engineered nanoparticles increases, continual reassessment will be needed to determine whether medical screening is warranted for workers producing or using these materials. NIOSH will continue to examine new research findings and update its recommendations on medical screening programs for workers exposed to nanoparticles. Appendices in the document provide further discussion on occupational health programs, instances where evidence for specific medical screening is lacking, and details on substances like nanoscale cadmium, which has existing medical screening recommendations for preventing or assessing lung and kidney toxicity.
